_doc: The Economist's notebook (core/economist.gd, ui/economist_screen.gd, an Almanac page). Each idea is met once: by the flag econ_<id> (set by the system that teaches it, or by dialogue) or, for kind 'history', by reading the Gazetteer plaque named in 'plaque'. 'lines' are what the page says; 'how' is the hint while it is still blank; the code adds worked examples from the game's real numbers (Economist.example). Keep every line short, true and wry.

ideas.title: Supply and demand
ideas.how: Sell a lot of one thing in one town and watch the price.
lines: A price is where what people want meets how much of it is about.
Flood a town with something and each one is worth a bit less to the next buyer. That's a glut.
Leave it a few days and the shelves empty, and the price creeps back. Or take it somewhere that's short.

ideas.title: Comparative advantage
ideas.how: Someone at Leeds Kirkgate Market has a puzzle about two stalls.
lines: David Ricardo's idea, from 1817: even if one place is better at making everything, both gain when each makes what it gives up least to make.
What counts is the cost in what else you could have made, not who is fastest.
It's why jute fibre is cheap in Dundee and dear down South, and why carrying it pays.

ideas.title: Opportunity cost
ideas.how: Buy a Deed and think about what else that money could have done.
lines: The real price of anything is the best thing you gave up to get it.
Money spent on a business can't also sit in savings earning interest, or buy a lease, or a very large number of pasties.
A good choice beats the next best one, not just nothing.

ideas.title: Simple and compound interest
ideas.how: Pay something into savings at the Building Society.
lines: Simple interest is paid on what you put in. Compound interest is paid on that and on the interest already added.
On savings, compounding is a slow, kind snowball. On a debt you don't pay down, it's the same snowball coming the other way.
Time does most of the work, which is why starting early matters more than starting big.

ideas.title: APR
ideas.how: Ask Pat at the Building Society what APR means, or take out a loan.
lines: APR is the annual percentage rate: what a year of borrowing costs once interest is charged on interest.
UK lenders must show it, so you can compare one loan with another on the same footing.
A small monthly rate can be a big yearly one. Read the yearly one.

ideas.title: Inflation
ideas.how: An old regular at Whitelock's in Leeds remembers Decimal Day.
lines: Inflation is prices rising across the board, which is the same thing as each pound buying less.
Britain went decimal on 15 February 1971: 240 old pence to the pound became 100 new ones.
Prices rose by about a quarter in 1975 alone. Today the Bank of England aims for 2% a year; in October 2022 it was 11.1%.

ideas.title: Auctions and the winner's curse
ideas.how: Win a lot at an Enclosure lease auction.
lines: At an auction the winner is whoever valued the lot most, and that is often whoever guessed highest.
If everyone's guess is a bit off, the highest guess is the most likely to be too high. That's the winner's curse.
The cure is dull: decide your top price before the bidding, and stop there.

ideas.title: Why the house always wins
ideas.how: Have a go at the Palace casino or the races.
lines: Every game pays a little less than the true odds. Over one night you might win. Over many, the sums win.
The gap is the house edge, or margin. It's the casino's rent, paid by everyone who plays, mostly the regulars.
If a bet costs you nothing to walk away from, walking away is the only one with no edge against you.

ideas.title: The Bank of England, 1694
lines: Founded in 1694 to lend money to William III's government for its war with France. The idea came from a Scot, William Paterson.
It has been on Threadneedle Street since 1734, hence the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street.
Since 1997 it, not ministers, sets the interest rate that steers inflation.

ideas.title: The South Sea Bubble, 1720
lines: The South Sea Company's shares soared past a thousand pounds in the summer of 1720, then fell to a fraction of that by the end of the year.
People bought because the price was rising, which made it rise, until it didn't. That is a bubble.
Isaac Newton is said to have lost a fortune in it.

ideas.title: Scottish banknotes
lines: The Bank of Scotland was set up by an Act of the Scottish Parliament in 1695, a year after the Bank of England.
Three Scottish banks still print their own notes. They're sterling all the same, whatever the shop in Dover says.

ideas.title: From the punt to the euro, 2002
lines: Ireland had its own pound, the punt, from 1928. It kept level with sterling until 1979, when the link was broken.
Ireland joined the euro in 1999, and euro notes and coins arrived on 1 January 2002. One euro was worth 0.787564 punts.
So the North and the Republic now spend different money on either side of an open border.

ideas.title: Northern Rock and the 2008 crash
lines: In September 2007 savers queued outside Northern Rock's branches to get their money out: a run on a British bank.
It was nationalised in February 2008. That September, Lehman Brothers collapsed in New York and the panic went worldwide.
Banks lend out most of what you pay in. That works as long as everyone doesn't want it back on the same day.

ideas.title: The Territories' own money
ideas.how: A plaque in Stanley, in the Falklands.
lines: The Falklands, Gibraltar and St Helena have their own pounds, fixed one for one with sterling.
Bermuda's dollar is fixed to the US dollar, the Caymans have their own dollar, the Virgin Islands and Turks and Caicos use the US dollar, and Pitcairn the New Zealand dollar.
Anguilla and Montserrat share the Eastern Caribbean dollar with their neighbours. Small places borrow a big currency's steadiness.
